text: hi. so i was watching a video about gta 3 and how they pulled off the rendering on 32mb of memory, and it is kinda funny because ive heard a few t imes you or another say the approach i am coming to in my head is a lot of the same approach that was used in gta 3/vc/sa, and it solidified how we can pull it off in our own approach at a pretty large scale. But im also wondering, how much of that might actually matter or not. One thing that we introduced before the most recent compile game to data approach (which is genuinely really really good where its at now), how big can we scale it in this approach before it starts to choke? the problem before with the v8 in the loop type of ordeal was it was quite random. id lag for no reason. and not lag when logs said i should be. we ended up doing the @cart/hmsc_massive_map_lab.tsx which revealed we could get away with a huge map, but only one way, which was one big mesh. Well lets try that again. effectively all i need you to do is just script up a map file so that i can run tools/rjit game play on it, and lets see if it chokes at all. I am thinking we are going to be able to fly with the new approach. like get away with a HUUUUUUUUUUUUGE map for almost nothing
resolution: Built a procedural-city scale lab so the user can run 'tools/rjit game play --massive [--blocks N]' to stress-test how big a world the no-V8 compile-to-data loader renders before it chokes. New generator cart/hmsc-int/compile/bakeMassiveGameFile.ts bakes through the EXACT real game-file pipe (createHmscMapfile -> writeGameFile, embedded player model/animation lumps, env) and swaps in a giant procedurally-generated INSTANCES lump — the whole city is one instanced unit-cube batch (the 'one big mesh' hmsc_massive_map_lab proved), zero V8 in the render loop. Wired --massive/--blocks selectors into game.ts play/shot via a shared installGameFileEnvelope helper + parseChoice, rebundled tools/rjit.js. Also raised world_loader.zig loadGameFile read cap 8MB->256MB (it was an arbitrary I/O guardrail, not a memory limit) so the lab probes the real GPU/physics ceiling. Validated JS-side bakes: 120 blocks=42,889 instances/3.75MB, 160=76,076/5.39MB, 200=118,706/7.51MB; fixed overhead is the 1.6MB player-model lump. Loader rebuild + live-window playtest is the user's build loop; left uncommitted pending the user's commit decision.
